newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia wakes up to promise of cheaper phone calls.
newsitem.headline: Australia wakes up to promise of cheaper phone calls.

text.p: Australian consumers were offered cut-rate telephone calls on Tuesday as the last regulatory shackles were lifted from the country's A$25 billion (US$18.75 billion) telecommunications sector.
In the first sign of a new competitive environment, Australia's third largest fixed-line telephone group AAPT Telecommunications Pty Ltd offered 60 percent off the price of long-distance call rates.
Other smaller players also promised cheaper calls to undercut the duopoly strangehold enjoyed until Tuesday's deregulation by state-owned Telstra Corp Ltd and Optus Communications Pty Ltd.

New entrants into the local telecoms market are soon expected -- there is no limit to the amount of carriers being allowed to operate in the deregulated Australian market, making it one of the freest telecoms market in the world.
Communications Minister Richard Alston said on Monday that about 30 companies were applying for carrier licences.

Alston said full deregulation could also stimulate economic growth as telecommunications was part of every sector of the economy. The economy would get a boost from lower prices and improved services, along with new jobs.
Australia's communications sector grew at 12 percent in the year to June 1996, compared with the nation's gross domestic product (GDP) rate of 4.4 percent.
Part of the strong growth in the telecoms sector is due to Australia's fondness for mobile phones . Almost one in for Australians own a cellular phone, one of the world's highest ownership rates.

Australia's mobile phone business was stimulated by the partial deregulation of the telecoms sector in 1992 when Optus and Britain's Vodafone Plc were allowed to offer mobile services. Optus was also allowed to compete against Telstra in the long distance fixed-line business.

The liberalisation of Australia's telecommunications sector is due to be followed later this year by the partial privatisation of Telstra Corp. The government is expected to raise a minimum of A$8 billion through the sale of one-third of the company's shares.

Other telecoms-related floats are also being planned including Optus, AAPT Telecommunications and U.S.-owned Northgate Australia and Worldxchange Australia Pty Ltd. So far no major Australian telecoms carriers are publicly listed.
